item.title: Shares: images, devices, directories
item.description:
A share serves one of three things: a disk image, a device node, or adirectory of the host. An image and a device carry a filesystem this program reads itself; a directory is the host’s own.

An image, and the filesystem inside it

The filesystem inside an image is worked out rather than declared.go-filesystems/detect reads the magic and hands back the driver that owns it: fat32, exfat, ext4, ntfs, ufs,iso9660, squashfs or hfsplus — every driver of the one shape,OpenReader(io.ReaderAt, int64), a filesystem at offset zero.

The four that cannot be sniffed

apfs, btrfs, xfs and zfs each open a disk image and pick a partition,so there is no magic at offset zero to find. A share says which:

share "photos" {
 image = "/srv/disk.img"
 filesystem = "xfs"
 partition = 2 # or leave it out: the driver takes the first data partition
}

HFS+ images are read-only unless a share opts in

Since v0.44.0 (hfsplus v0.9.0) a share whose image holds HFS+ is opened for writing, like FAT, exFAT and ext4: a client can create, change and delete files, and the times, modes and owners it sets are stored. Before, an HFS+ image was opened read-only. The image is read into memory when the share opens and every change is written back to the file.

Off by default since v0.45.1. hfsplus v0.9.0 is not crash-safe: it rewrites the whole image on every operation and never marks the volume as in use while it does, so a crash or power loss in the middle of a write leaves a torn image that still says it was cleanly unmounted, and nothing checks it at the next mount. On a journaled volume the fix needs more than writing in place. v0.44.0 and v0.45.0 wrote by default (up to 256 MiB); since v0.45.1 an HFS+ share is servedread-only unless it sets hfsplus_writable_max. The fix is go-filesystems/hfsplus#34; the default can come back when it is released. To opt in, set a size (and back the image up first), accepting this risk and the costs below.

What it costs. hfsplus v0.9.0 holds the whole image in memory and rewrites the whole image on every operation (a create, a write, a rename, a Chtimes),so the memory of a share is the size of its image, and so is the I/O of every change (go-filesystems/hfsplus#33 is the real fix). A share therefore opens an HFS+ image for writing only up to hfsplus_writable_max, which is "0" (never)by default (a number of bytes, or one with K, M, G or T):

share "mac" {
 image = "/srv/mac.img"
 hfsplus_writable_max = "256M" # opt in
}

With the default, above the cap, or when the size is unknown, the share opensread-only, still with range reads and times, and the server writes one line naming the image and the reason, for instance with no setting:

/srv/mac.img is an HFS+ volume and hfsplus_writable_max is 0, the default: hfsplus v0.9.0 is not crash-safe (a crash mid-write can leave a torn image marked clean), so HFS+ images are written only when a share sets a size, so mac is read-only

and above the size:

/srv/mac.img is an HFS+ volume and it is 1073741824 bytes, over hfsplus_writable_max (268435456 bytes): a writable HFS+ image is held in memory and rewritten whole on every change, so mac is read-only

A journaled volume (made by hdiutil create -fs "Journaled HFS+" or by macOS) is written only when its journal is empty, which is what a clean unmount leaves. A journal that holds transactions, or one that cannot be verified, would be replayed by macOS over what the server writes, so the driver refuses it and the share opens read-only instead. The server keeps starting; it writes one line when the share opens, naming the image, the share and why:

/srv/mac.img is an HFS+ volume and its journal holds transactions (hfsplus: journaled volume with a journal that is not empty: transactions pending (start 17408, end 34816)), so mac is read-only

To make such a share writable, have the journal replayed first: mount the image on a Mac and eject it cleanly, or run fsck_hfs on it. (The driver has no journal check that works without the image in memory, so this one case reads the image, up to the cap, before it falls back.) A share with read_only = true, a device and a partition never try the writable open.

Another writer. The image is flushed whole, so a second writer would be overwritten by the next flush. A writable open takes an exclusive advisoryflock on the image (Linux, macOS and the BSDs); if another process holds it,for instance a second fileshare on the same image, the share opens read-only and says so. The lock is advisory: a macOS mount does not take it, and on other platforms there is no lock.

⛔ Do not write an image that is mounted, by this server or by anything else: neither side knows about the other’s changes. Serve an image that nothing else has open.

A writable image the OS has mounted is served read-only

Since v0.45.0, before any writable image share (FAT32, exFAT, ext4, UFS,btrfs, XFS, ZFS, HFS+: whatever the driver) is opened for writing, the server asks the OS whether it has that image attached or mounted. If it has, the share opens read-only, is marked read-only, and the server writes one line naming the image, the OS’s device and mount, and the share:

/srv/disk.img is in use by the OS (/dev/loop3, mounted at /mnt/disk), and a second writer would corrupt it, so disk is read-only

The advisory flock above cannot do this: the OS takes no lock when it mounts an image. The image is matched by device and inode, never by comparing path strings,so a symbolic link or a hard link to the mounted file is caught too.

OS How it is asked
Linux /sys/block/loop*/loop/backing_file of each loop device (what mount -o loop, losetup and udisks make); the mount point comes from /proc/self/mountinfo. An attached loop device counts even when nothing is mounted on it.
macOS hdiutil info -plist, the image-path of each attached image, one call per load, bounded by a 15 s timeout. An image attached with -nomount counts.
FreeBSD, other BSDs, Windows Cannot be detected. The share is writable, as before.

When the check itself fails (no /sys/block in a container, hdiutil missing or timing out, output that is not a property list), nobody knows whether the image is mounted. image_mount_unknown decides:

share "disk" {
 image = "/srv/disk.img"
 image_mount_unknown = "read_only" # the default; "write" serves it writable anyway
}

The default is read_only: a read-only share is a visible state with a log line that names its cause, and a person can fix it; a writable share under a mount corrupts both sides’ data, and nobody sees it until later. write is for a host where the check cannot work (a container with no sysfs) and nobody mounts images. An image the OS is known to have mounted is read-only whatever this says.A backing path the check cannot read (permission denied, a symbolic-link loop) is“could not be judged”, not “another image”: it goes to the same setting. Only a path that is not there is skipped. On Linux a loop device whose backing file was deleted is matched through the kernel’s own record (LOOP_GET_STATUS64) when the process may open /dev/loopN, and is otherwise not matched.

What the check cannot see

  • A mount made after the share opened the image. The check runs when an image is opened: at start, for a share created through the admin API, and when a reload rebuilds the shares (a change of people or lists) and finds the image mounted since, in which case that share gets a read-only open of its own. A reload that changes nothing does not look again, and nothing watches for a laterhdiutil attach or mount -o loop. Stop the share, or restart the server,before mounting an image it serves writable.
  • Mounts that go through no loop device or hdiutil: qemu-nbd -c (an nbd device), FUSE mounts (fuse2fs, guestmount), and a virtual machine or other program that has the image open.
  • Other operating systems (see the table), and a Linux loop device attached in another mount namespace.
  • A share made read-only because of a mount stays read-only on a reload even if the mount has gone; restart it to open it for writing again.

A partition, for any filesystem

A disk image holding FAT32, ext4 or exFAT has a partition table in front of it as often as one holding XFS does — and detection reads offset zero, where a partitioned image has the table. So the partition is chosen first, and the driver is handed a view of it:

share "photos" {
 image = "/srv/disk.img"
 partition_label = "photos" # what lsblk calls PARTLABEL
}

Three ways to name one, and only one may be given — two that disagree would serve whichever the code tried first:
partition = 2 counting from 1, the way partitioning tools print them
partition_label = "photos" the GPT partition name
partition_uuid = "…" the GPT unique GUID — Linux’s PARTUUID

An index moves

A disk repartitioned, a tool that writes entries in another order, an image restored with one partition fewer — and partition = 2 names something else, silently, because a filesystem is still found there. A label or a UUID names the partition itself, which is why fstabs stopped using indexes years ago. The index is here for MBR images, which have neither.

A share that chose a partition is read-only, and says so at startup: the driver’s offsets are the partition’s while the file underneath is the whole disk, so a write would land at that offset from the start of the image — on the partition table, as often as not.

Naming a filesystem turns detection off

That is the point, and it is the risk

The image is opened as that or refused. A FAT32 image told it is XFS does not become an XFS share; it fails to start, saying what it was asked to open it as.

filesystem is accepted for the sniffable ones too, and then the two are compared: a share that says ext4 over a FAT32 image is refused with the share says ext4 and the image holds fat32. That is how a site refuses a misdetection rather than discovering one later.check marks a named driver with an asterisk, because that row was not recognised — it was asserted.

A device, not only an image 

share "photos" {
 image = "/dev/sda" # a device node, not a file
}

No privilege is involved. Nothing here mounts anything — thego-filesystems drivers read ext4, xfs and the rest in user space — so there is no mount(2) and therefore noCAP_SYS_ADMIN. Opening a device is an ordinary open(2), governed by the permissions on the node:

owner mode enough
Linux /dev/sda root:disk 0660 membership of disk
macOS /dev/disk0 root:operator 0640 membership of operator, plus Full Disk Access

A refusal says which group, rather than permission denied — the answer is never sudo.

⛔ A device share is read-only, for the same reason as a share that chose a partition: writing to a live disk is not a decision to make on your behalf.

The device is opened exclusively, and that is about correctness, not caution

If the kernel has a filesystem mounted from it, the filesystem’s page cache holds newer metadata than the device does — so a raw reader sees a directory block from before an update beside an inode block from after it,a state that never existed on disk at any one moment. O_EXCL on a block device is the kernel’s own primitive for “nobody else, a mount included”;it is what mkfs and fsck use. A device in use is refused, by name, with the reason.

Two things were measured rather than assumed:

  • Stat().Size() is 0 for a device, so the length is asked of the device itself. Seeking to the end answers on Linux and returns 0 with no error on macOS, which is why Darwin uses DKIOCGETBLOCKCOUNT instead.
  • A raw node (/dev/rdiskN, or O_DIRECT on Linux) refuses an unaligned read, and reading a two-byte field at offset 11 is what parsing a FAT BPBis. Reads to a device are rounded out to whole blocks; without that,/dev/rdisk4 reported unknown filesystem.

A directory, not only an image

Since v0.8.0 a share may serve a directory of the host — a container’s volume,say — instead of an image:

share "photos" {
 directory = "/data/photos"
 allow = ["@family"]
}

It is go-filesystems/osfs, which reaches the tree through an os.Root: .. that climbs out, an absolute path, and a symbolic link leading out are refused by the kernel-backed root,not by a string test. A client may create a link to /etc; nothing will follow it. A FIFO planted in the tree is refused rather than left to hang the server.

One share may not hold another (since v0.17.0)

A directory share whose tree holds another share’s image or directory isrefused at start, and by the admin API: whoever may use the outer share would read and write the inner one without being allowed it —anonymous NFS included. So are two shares on the same source, except two different partitions of one disk image.

Not behind the image lock

An image driver owns one file and promises nothing about two calls at once,which is why every image is wrapped in one lock.A host tree is the kernel’s, which serialises what must be serialised per call and no more; one mutex in front of every file of every client would be the slowest thing a file server can do.

⛔ A share has an image or a directory, never both, and never neither.filesystem and partition are for an image: a directory share naming one is refused, because saying one means the share was meant to be an image.read_only = true works on a directory as on an image; a share that says it and also lists writers is refused, because read_only would win.

The capacity a client is told is that of the filesystem the tree lives on; a platform that cannot say leaves it at zero, which the protocols read as“unknown” rather than “full”.

What SMB does with a time it cannot store

A time a client sets that the storage cannot keep is ignored by default.Since v0.42.0 a share can choose, with unstorable_times. A time is unstorable when it is a CreationTime that differs from the reported one, a ChangeTime sent alone, or an access or write time on an image whose driver cannot set times(NTFS, APFS, ISO 9660, SquashFS; a host directory and a FAT, exFAT, ext4 or HFS+ image store those):

share "photos" {
 directory = "/data/photos"
 unstorable_times = "log" # "ignore" (the default), "refuse" or "log"
}

refuse answers the client with an error, and log writes one line naming the share and the path. The exact cases, per kind of share, are inReal file times.

item.title: Directories served as each person
item.description:
Ordinarily one fileshare process serves everybody as one account: fileshare decides who may do what, and every file it creates belongs to that account.A directory share can instead be served as each person. Whoever logged in has their files opened by a process running with their uid, gid and groups, so the kernel applies the tree’s permissions and what they create belongs to them.

identity {
 service_user = "fileshare" # the account the protocols are served as
 min_uid = 1000 # the default; uid 0 is refused whatever this says
 min_gid = 1000
 deny_uids = [65534]
 idle = "2m" # how long an unused worker is kept
}

share "home" {
 directory = "/srv/home"
 identity = "system"
}

Three processes

fileshare serve must be started as root. It stays root only to start each person’s worker. Everything that faces the network runs in a second process, as service_user.

process runs as does
the launcher (fileshare serve) root binds the listeners, starts the front, starts workers when the front asks. It speaks no protocol.
the front service_user, with that account’s groups speaks the protocols and authenticates, as serve always has. For such a share it asks the launcher for a person and a share, never a uid or a path.
a worker the person serves one share to the front, over a socket the launcher handed across

A worker first checks that it is running as exactly the expected uid, gid and groups, and that setuid(0) fails. Only then does it open the tree,through an os.Root. One worker serves all of that person’s connections to the share, over SFTP and WebDAV alike, and it stops once nothing has used it for idle. When the server stops, the workers stop with it.

Who a person is on this system

The launcher resolves the person itself, in this order:

  1. The directory, if it carries uidNumber and gidNumber:

    • a user block’s attributes = { uidNumber = "2001", gidNumber = "2001" };
    • an LDAP source with attributes = ["uidNumber", "gidNumber"];
    • an SQL source’s users_attributes query.

    The supplementary groups are the groups that list the person (a group block’s members, memberUid) and those the person names (memberOf),each by its gidNumber. A group without one is not a system group.

  2. /etc/passwd and /etc/group, by name.

Refused: uid 0, gid 0, (uid_t)-1, a uid below min_uid, a primary gid below min_gid, and every uid in deny_uids. A supplementary group belowmin_gid is left out, and the log says so. A person found in neither place is refused too: there is no shared fallback account. A person the identity provider vouches for gets a worker only withlocal_names, which makes their name a local one.

So a front that has been taken over can ask only for a person who exists and is allowed, on a share that exists. It still decides who has authenticated, and the launcher cannot check that for it.

What a client sees

SFTP WebDAV
a worker is taken at login, for the whole connection per request; locks live as long as the worker does
the launcher refuses the person the share is not in their tree (a tree with nothing in it is a refused login) 403
no worker can be started the same 503

The reason goes to the server’s log, never to the client.

Not over SMB, NFS or S3 yet

They refuse such a share, and check says so. SMB and NFS need a filesystem per session in their libraries. NFS will only ever do it under Kerberos, because AUTH_UNIX is the client’s own claim (RFC 5531 §14).

What it asks of the system

  • Unix: Linux, the BSDs and macOS. On Windows the share is refused.
  • Readable by service_user: the configuration and every file it names(password files, host key, certificates), since the front reads them.
  • Executable by the people: the binary, since each worker runs it as its person.
  • A restart to add or change such a share. The launcher reads the configuration once, and refuses a share it does not know rather than let the front serve it.
  • --isolate does not go with it.

The design, and why each choice was made, is indocs/identity.md.
